title: Does size matter?
question: Do larger sums draw more no votes than smaller ones?
finding: A little, on small numbers. Files naming $10 million or more drew a no in 39 of 1,064 cases (3.7%); files naming less, in 28 of 1,236 (2.3%). Leaving out noes that were part of a same-day list, the figures are 26 of 1,064 (2.4%) and 18 of 1,236 (1.5%); chance alone would give a gap that wide about 9% of the time, so it is suggestive at most. Files with no single amount in the title, which include the annual budget, have the highest share: 57 of 1,183 (4.8%). Larger files are also the ones that come with a written analyst’s report: 89.2% of those of $100 million or more introduced since 2019, against 10.4% of those under $1 million.
how: Each file with a final vote is placed in a band by the total its title names. The last three columns cover contract, lease and grant files introduced since 2019 and count those with a Budget and Legislative Analyst report among their attachments on the Board’s site (the reports were collected for files heard by the budget committees). The chance figure is an exact test on the two-by-two table of files of $10 million or more against smaller ones, with and without a no outside a same-day list.
limits: A unanimous vote is the ordinary result and no sign of anything wrong. 3,419 of the 3,483 files were recommended by a committee before the Board voted, 900 accept a grant or gift, and 1,104 amend or extend an agreement already in place. Of the 770 files of $10 million or more introduced since 2019, 650 carry a report by the Board’s Budget and Legislative Analyst among their attachments, so a vote with no dissent can follow written scrutiny at the committee stage. A no vote is ordinary; the vote pages give no reasons, and dissent can reflect a disagreement about policy or the budget rather than doubt about the organization named in the file. Dollar figures are the totals named in file titles: an agreement amended twice is counted at each new total, rent and accepted grants are money coming to the City as well as money going out, and budget ordinances name no single figure, so a sum of title dollars measures what the titles name, not money spent. The $10 million and $25 million marks are the lines discussed on the page about money that never reaches a vote; a band is a way of sorting titles, not a legal test applied to each file. For 332 roll calls the Clerk’s vote page says “by the following vote” and lists no member, 306 of them dated 2016-04-13 to 2016-07-26; 315 were read instead from the vote lines in the Clerk’s published minutes of the same meeting, and 17 remain without member votes and are counted nowhere here. 1 money file (160358) whose final passage is among them is left out of the counts, and none is counted as unanimous. 104 of the final votes counted here were read from the minutes. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
